zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review sources: Native scan, Bibliothèque nationale de France / Gallica. Secondary lexical check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, licensed CC BY 4.0 (official release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The transcription corrections and English notes are original scan-grounded review work; the lexical data and generated reading hints do not determine diplomatic spelling.

lines.note: Chi completes cutçu- from f433, followed by tengoo, finishing the three-illness list. The Portuguese names leprosy and gota coral, then begins another comparison; outra restores the visible t omitted by OCR. These are the source's historical disease labels, not modern diagnoses.
Como gota coral completes the description of the third condition as resembling the second. This short continuation closes Sanbiǒ from the preceding page.

runs.text: Sanbô. Mitçuno tacara. i, But, fô, ſô.

lines.note: Sanboo is explained as the three treasures, followed by But, foo, and soo. The three abbreviated Japanese religious names and the comma after i are copied as printed; the final punctuation is upright with the list.
Fotoque, Ley, and Bonzo gloss the three treasures in the dictionary's terminology. Sanboo no sute- begins the example of a person abandoned by them, completed below.
Mono completes sutemono. The Portuguese calls the person lost or abandoned, with deſem- continued on the following row.

runs.text: parado deſtas tres couſas ſanctas: poſto q̃ cõmũ-

lines.note: Parado completes deſem-parado, abandoned by these three sacred things. The qualification beginning poſto q̃ cõmũ- introduces how the expression is ordinarily used.

runs.text: mente ſe toma no vulgo per homẽ inutil.

lines.note: Mente completes cõmũ-mente. Common usage takes the phrase to mean a useless person; the scan supports inutil rather than OCR inatil, while per and homẽ remain unnormalized.

runs.text: Certa laya de teſtos, ou bacios de

lines.note: Sanboojen is described as a kind of earthenware dish or shallow vessel. The following rows explain the three foods and the placement at the meal.

runs.text: barro com tres iguarias que ſe poem diante do

lines.note: The earthenware holds three dishes of food that are placed before the diner. The Portuguese relative clause continues on the next row.
Que eſtà à meſa identifies the person seated at table. The two grave-marked vowels are retained according to their local impressions.

Sanbon cufai is explained by an analogy with three hierarchies and nine ranks. The source's comparative como is important: it presents an explanatory parallel rather than an identity of religious systems.

runs.text: ue choros, ou ordẽs de gente celeſte, &c.

lines.note: Ve completes no-ve; the nine are described as choirs or orders of celestial people. The Portuguese religious vocabulary continues the preceding analogy.

runs.text: A terceira parte, ou das tres par-

lines.note: Sanbuichi means one third. The Portuguese begins a second formulation, one of three parts, with par- divided at the line end.
Tes completes par-tes, and a hũa specifies one of them. The nasal abbreviation in hũa is retained.
Sanbut is explained by Dainichi no koto, a reference to Dainichi. The Portuguese introduces it as the name of a particular religious figure rather than expanding the compound literally.
Certo Fotoque completes that identification. Fotoque occurs within the Portuguese explanation and is not another headword here.
This Sanka is yama no shita, the foot of a mountain. The scan shows the historical double-vowel pee, not the draft's single pe; the Portuguese phrase continues below.
Monte completes the foot-of-the-mountain gloss. S labels written usage and closes this sense of Sanca. The terminal S. is an upright written-register label.

runs.text: Oir a algũa parte em andas.

lines.note: The next Sanca is going somewhere in a litter or sedan chair. The compact Oir setting and written-register S are retained rather than modernized. The final S. is upright, outside the italic gloss.
This Sanca is yama no ie, mountain dwellings. The Portuguese broadens the location to houses in the countryside on the following row.
Que eſtão nos campos adds houses situated in the fields or country. S closes this written-register entry, not the next mountain-and-river sense. The standalone S. is an upright register label.
Sanca, alternatively xenga, is explained by yama and kawa, mountains and rivers. The printed c in Sanca and x in xenga are retained rather than harmonized with Sanga later in the page.
This Sanca is permission to go out, explained by mairu itoma. The Portuguese licẽça is printed with a nasal abbreviation, and S again marks written usage. The terminal S. is set upright.
Sankaku is misumi, a triangle or something having three corners. The Portuguese definition continues with the number of corners below.
Tres cantos completes the three-cornered definition. The short row remains separate from the following adjective.
Sankakuna is the adjectival form, triangular. The Portuguese gives its meaning directly in a single line.
Sankakuni is labeled as the corresponding adverb. No missing Portuguese gloss is supplied after Adu.; the printed short entry is complete as it stands.
Sankai means mountains and sea, explained by yama and umi. Vt introduces an example of their prized products on the following row.
Sankai no chinbut, kokudo no kwashi refers to prized products of land and sea and fruits of various lands. The checked ending in chinbut is preserved, and Co- begins the Portuguese translation below.

runs.text: meres exquiſitos domar, & da terra, & fru-

lines.note: Meres completes Co-meres: fine foods from sea and land. The close domar setting remains literal, and fru- begins fruitas on the next row.
Itas completes fru-itas, fruits from different kingdoms or regions. This continues the example rather than introducing another food headword.
Sankan means reckoning or computation, with kangaye and kangayuru as principal Japanese explanations. The Portuguese gives computar and continues with an alternative expression below.
The Portuguese alternative is fazer contas. Sancanni taxitaru fito is the example of a person skilled in reckoning; its printed taxitaru is retained rather than silently regularized.

runs.text: Homem destro na arte de contar.

lines.note: The translation describes a person dexterous in the art of counting. The close st type in destro does not require a spelling change.
Sankanja is a good calculator or arithmetician. The letter after ari is t, giving arithmetico, rather than the OCR's arilhmetico.

runs.text: Cha großeiro q̃ ſe da ẽ terras montuoſas.

lines.note: Sancha is coarse tea growing in mountainous places. The nasal abbreviations in q̃ and ẽ, the sharp-s type in großeiro, and the historical montuoſas are retained.
Sanchaku, explained by mairi tsuku, denotes arrival. The Portuguese reads chegar, not abegar; chega- continues into the noun chegada on the next row.
Da completes chega-da: someone's arrival at a place. Dalguem remains a single printed word, and this indented row belongs to Sanchacu.
Sanchô is a bird of the mountains or wild country, explained by yama no tori. The headword's circumflex and the sharp-s type in Paßaro remain as printed.
Sanchǔ names three celebrated Chinese books. The caron over the final u is retained; the entry does not identify the individual titles, so none are supplied.
This second Sanchǔ is yama no uchi, within mountain country or woodland. The spelling is distinguished from the preceding book-title entry by its explanation, not by a fabricated diacritic.

runs.text: deſerto. Item, no Ximo, Desterro. Vt,

lines.note: The definition continues with wilderness and adds the regional Ximo sense of exile. San- begins the Japanese example that continues below; Ximo is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Chǔ completes San-chǔ suru, to be exiled. The Portuguese translation confirms that this is the regional sense introduced on the previous row.
Sanchǔ jin denotes an exile. The final vowel's caron is damaged but belongs with the immediately preceding Sanchǔ entry; jin ends in n, not u, and the regional label X. is wholly upright.

runs.text: Sanco. Mitçu no to. i, Me, mimi, cuchi.

lines.note: Sanko is explained as three doors: eyes, ears, and mouth. The explanatory phrase reads Mitçu no to, with u after ç and the printed separation before no retained. Me, mimi, and cuchi remain Japanese explanations, not Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Tres portas dos ſentidos. ſ. olhos, ouuidos, boca.

lines.note: The Portuguese enumerates the three sensory doors as eyes, ears, and mouth. The apparent OCR word ſcolhos is actually the abbreviation ſ. followed by olhos.
Sanko wo hisomuru is illustrated as closing the three doors. The last word begins por, not per, and continues as tas at the top of the next column; no unprinted hyphen is supplied.

runs.text: tas. i, calarſe & estar com atenção.

lines.note: Tas completes the preceding column's por-tas. The explanatory sense is to remain silent and attentive, not a new headword at the top of this column.

runs.text: O ir diante do ſenhor, & aßistir, ou eſ-

lines.note: Sankô concerns attending before one's lord. The enlarged type reads aßistir, with the short s adjoining t, rather than aßislir; eſ- continues below.
Tar completes eſ-tar: to remain ready for the lord's service. The close printed ſeuſeruiço is retained rather than respaced from modern usage.
Sancǒ, here explained by yama wo yuku, means passing or walking through mountains. The caron distinguishes this entry graphically from neighboring Sancô forms.
The mountainous route completes the definition above. The terminal S. is an upright written-register label, outside the italic Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Ir praticar com algũa peßoa de reſpeito.

lines.note: This Sancô means going to converse with a respected person. The circumflex belongs to this headword, and the nasal mark in algũa remains over u.

runs.text: Sancǒ. Mitçuno vôzzuna. i, cunxin, fu-

lines.note: Sancǒ introduces the three major bonds, mitçuno vôzzuna. Cunxin is the lord-retainer relation; fu- continues below as fuxi, followed by fǔfu.

runs.text: Tres grãdes lianças. ſ. de ſenhor

lines.note: Xi completes fu-xi, the father-child relation; fǔfu is the marital relation. The Portuguese has grãdes, not grãdas, and ſ. de, not ſa de, introducing the first bond's explanation.
This completes the three paired relations: lord and servant, father and son, husband and wife. The vowel in filho is i, not the OCR's u; pay and molher retain their historical spelling.
Sanco, alternatively ſango, names a metal implement. The cramped metalque remains as in the aligned reading; the alternative's long ſ is not a lowercase l.

The metal implement serves in non-Christian religious ceremonies, described here by the source's gentilicas. The sentence continues the preceding entry, without identifying a more specific object than the print does.
Sankoku is mountains and valleys, yama and tani. The Portuguese reads montes, not mentes, and reverses the order of the two Japanese nouns.

runs.text: Item, Nome de hũ liuro de poeſia da China.

lines.note: An additional sense is the name of a Chinese poetry book. The row begins Item without the draft's unsupported paragraph mark; the title is not expanded beyond the headword.
Sandai is a Buddhist term for three substances or entities, mitçuno tai. The damaged consonant is b in ſubstancias, not l; the standalone Bup. label remains upright.

runs.text: de que ſe fala no Buppô.

lines.note: The three substances are discussed within Buddhist teaching. The visible mark over the final o of Buppô is a circumflex, not a grave, and the word is embedded in Portuguese prose.
A separate sandai means going to the imperial palace, dairi ni mairu. The Portuguese prints Rey with an e, not the OCR's Ry.

runs.text: Hum liuro de poeſia de Iapão.

lines.note: Sandaixǔ designates a Japanese poetry book or collection. The country's name starts with capital I in Iapão; Hum is printed unabbreviated, unlike nearby hũ.
Sandan is explained by fome cataru, speaking in praise. Dal- begins the object of that praise and continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: gũa couſa com louuor: posto que comummente

lines.note: Gũa completes dal-gũa: speaking of something with praise. The following qualification introduces the term's more general current use; the historical comummente is preserved.

runs.text: ſe toma por falar, ou tratar dalgũa couſa.

lines.note: The qualification says that the word commonly means simply speaking or treating of something. This broader usage should not be replaced by a narrower modern sense of sandan.
Sandô, explained as yama-warawa, is a boy roaming mountain or woodland country. The headword visibly abbreviates the nasal as Sãdô rather than printing an n; the circumflex over o is separate.

runs.text: Sandocu. i, Ton, Iin, Chi. Bup. Mitçuno do

lines.note: Sandoku names the three Buddhist poisons, ton, jin, and chi. The explanatory phrase is Mitçuno, not Mitçuuo; do continues as cu below without an added hyphen. Printed Iin is retained as the historical consonantal-I spelling.

runs.text: Tres raizes de peccados. ſ. Cubiça, Ira,

lines.note: Cu completes do-cu. The Portuguese begins the enumeration of three roots of sin with greed and anger, retaining its Christian interpretative vocabulary rather than substituting a modern doctrinal formula.

runs.text: Ignorancia, q̃ impedem a ſaluação, & por ißo

lines.note: Ignorance completes the threefold list. The source says these obstruct salvation and continues into its explanation of why they are called poisons; the tilde in q̃ is retained.
The clause completes the explanation that greed, anger, and ignorance are called three poisons. Peçonhas is the historical Portuguese term, not a separate Japanese expression.

runs.text: Certa feição de testo de barro.

lines.note: Sandoiri is a particular form of earthenware lid or cover. The printed testo is retained as the object term, without adding a more specific modern utensil identification.
Sane is a fruit stone or seed, glossed by caroço and peuide. The short entry is complete before the separately repeated Sane below.

runs.text: Ferros vraxados de preto como cabeças

lines.note: The next Sane describes black-lacquered iron elements of armor, likened to nail heads. Vraxados is retained as the source's lacquer-related Portuguese spelling rather than modernized.

runs.text: de prègos das armas, entre os quaes fazem aie-

lines.note: The armor elements are connected by a multicolored weave described across the line break. Enlargement still favors the printed aie- with an i-like type, although the context suggests tecedura; this anomalous draft reading is retained with that caveat. Prègos has a grave.

Cedura continues the preceding anomalous aie- sequence, and varias cores describes the colors of the lacing. The intended textile connection does not authorize silently repairing the preceding printed letters.
Sanekazura is compared with ivy. The Portuguese prints era, an older form in this comparison, rather than the modern spelling hera; no botanical species is imposed on the gloss.
Sanga, alternatively Xenga, is mountains and rivers, yama and kawa. The final Portuguese noun reads rios, not riou; this repeated geographical entry is not deleted as a duplicate.

runs.text: Sangacu. i. Ienxǔno ſatoriuo manabu coto.

lines.note: Sangaku is learning or seeking the insight of the Zen school, explained by Ienxǔno ſatoriuo manabu coto. The final stop is visible at the right edge; consonantal I in Ienxǔ is preserved.

runs.text: O ir tomar os põtos de meditação a certas horas

lines.note: The Portuguese describes going at set hours to receive subjects for meditation. The final word is plural horas; its last s is present before the rule, not missing from the line.

runs.text: do mestre dos Ienxus. ¶ Item, Os pontos, ou

lines.note: The meditation subjects come from the Zen teacher. A paragraph mark then introduces an additional nominal sense, the subjects or points themselves; Ienxus occurs within Portuguese prose.

This completes the sense of Zen meditation topics. The unusual da ſeitasdos is retained rather than grammatically repaired; Iẽxùs starts with capital I and has the printed nasal and grave marks. The example visibly abbreviates the nasal as Sãgacu.
The example is translated as learning these meditations. It belongs to the preceding Zen sense rather than the geographical Sangacu that follows.
A separate sangaku means a mountain or hill, yama and oka. The Portuguese diminutive has an n in outeirinho, which the OCR omitted.
Ou morro completes the geographical gloss with another Portuguese term for a hill. The short continuation remains a separate physical row.

runs.text: Sangai. Bup. Mitçuno cai. ſ. Yoccai, xi-

lines.note: Sangai introduces the Buddhist three realms, mitçuno cai. Yoccai names the first; xi- begins xiqicai on the next row. Bup. is a domain label, not part of the Japanese enumeration.
Qicai completes xi-qicai, followed by muxiqi cai, the form and formless realms. The Portuguese noun starts mũ-, with m rather than n, and continues as dos below.

runs.text: dos de que ſe fala no Buppô.

lines.note: Dos completes mũ-dos, worlds discussed in Buddhist teaching. Buppô has a circumflex and belongs to the italic Portuguese phrase; the draft's isolated upright final vowel is removed.
Sanga nichi means three days. The example joins Xǒguachi to the following expression, and the final a of ſã- visibly carries a nasal abbreviation; its continuation is damaged or defective below.

The continuation visibly reads g nichi, with a gap and no secure vowel after g; the draft's e is not affirmed by enlargement. The intended phrase concerns the first three days of New Year, but the defective spacing is retained. In the gloss Xǒguachi has a caron, not i.
The first three days are described as festival days. This short continuation closes the New Year example without adding another calendar term.
Sangin is going to a military camp, cin ye mairu. The source separates Cinye and mairu; the Portuguese preposition reads pera, not peru.

runs.text: aguerra, ou pera onde eſta o exercito quando

lines.note: The destination is war or the place where the army is stationed. Exercito has e after x, not c; the close printed aguerra is preserved. The qualification continues on the final row.

The final clause specifies that this is not the first occasion. The word is primeira, not primeha, in the tightly set aprimeira. The separate San- at the far right is a catchword, not part of this sentence.
